claim: Standard featurewise confound removal by linear regression, applied before nonlinear ML models, can amplify null or moderate true effects to near-perfect prediction accuracy -- a documented case of a de-confounding procedure increasing a reported effect.
stance_target: kill hunt for N9: does a de-confounding audit increasing an effect have ML precedent?
scope_conditions: Nonlinear ML models (e.g. random forests, kernel methods) applied after linear confound regression; demonstrated via simulation and a clinical dataset
quoted_support: "this common deconfounding approach can leak information such that what are null or moderate effects become amplified to near-perfect prediction when nonlinear ML approaches are subsequently applied."

claim: The paper's own authors diagnose an effect-size increase following confound removal as a bias artifact ('confound-leakage'), not a legitimate corrected finding, and demonstrate this concretely by showing ADHD-prediction accuracy is overestimated when depression is used as the confound.
stance_target: the implicit assumption that a corrected/de-confounded statistic increasing is presumptively valid
scope_conditions: Clinical dataset: ADHD prediction from speech-derived features with depression as confound
quoted_support: "We demonstrate the real-world importance of confound-leakage by analyzing a clinical dataset where accuracy is overestimated for predicting attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) with depression as a confound."

claim: The paper concludes with an explicit caution against naive use of standard confound-removal approaches in ML workflows, given the risk of leakage-driven inflation of apparent effects.
stance_target: general methodological caution relevant to any de-confounding audit claiming an increased effect
quoted_support: "Our results have wide-reaching implications for implementation and deployment of ML workflows and beg caution against naive use of standard confound removal approaches."
